Basel
BAH-zel
n. (the Rhine city of the great presses, reformed under Oecolampadius in 1529, and the printing house and asylum of Reformation Europe)
Latin Basilea, from the Greek basileia, a royal place, the Roman Basilia on the Rhine; German Basel, French Bâle.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Basel is the Swiss city whose presses mattered more than its politics. Standing where the Rhine turns north, with a university from 1460 and the greatest printing houses north of Venice, it published Erasmus's Greek New Testament at Froben's press in 1516, the text from which Luther and Tyndale translated; Erasmus himself lived and died there. Johannes Oecolampadius, preaching from 1522, led the Reformation to its conclusion in February 1529, when the guilds forced the council's hand, the images were taken out of the minster, and the mass was abolished; the Basel Confession of 1534 followed, and the First Helvetic Confession was drafted there in 1536. The city then became an asylum. Italians fleeing the Roman inquisition, French fleeing the Valois, and Englishmen fleeing Mary all found houses and work in Basel, and its printers put out what no other city would, including Castellio's arguments against the burning of heretics. The dictionary enters Basel because the two things it gave the Reformation were a Greek text and a refuge, and because it is the one Reformed city that kept printing the men the Reformed authorities elsewhere wanted silenced.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a press as the business of printing; an asylum as a place of refuge; a minster as the church of a monastery; and a guild as an incorporated society of tradesmen.

expand to see more

PRESS, n. A machine for printing; the art or business of printing and publishing; the printing house itself.

ASYLUM, n. A sanctuary or place of refuge; any place of retreat and security.

MINSTER, n. A monastery; an ecclesiastical convent or fraternity; a cathedral church.

GUILD, n. A society, fraternity or corporation, associated for some common purpose, as of trade.

CONSCIENCE, n. Internal or self-knowledge, or judgment of right and wrong; the faculty by which we judge of the moral quality of actions.

Key Scripture

Isa 55:11 — "So shall my word be that goeth forth out of my mouth: it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please, and it shall prosper in the thing whereto I sent it."

Heb 4:12 — "For the word of God is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword, piercing even to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit, and of the joints and marrow, and is a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart."

Mat 13:29 — "But he said, Nay; lest while ye gather up the tares, ye root up also the wheat with them."

Rom 14:4 — "Who art thou that judgest another man's servant? to his own master he standeth or falleth. Yea, he shall be holden up: for God is able to make him stand."

Modern Corruption

Rhine city of the Froben press and Erasmus's Greek New Testament, reformed under Oecolampadius in 1529, and the asylum and printing house of Reformation Europe.

expand to see more

The corruption to be named is the execution of men for their doctrine by Protestant magistrates, and Basel is where it was first argued against in print. Sebastian Castellio, professor of Greek there, published after Servetus's burning at Geneva in 1553 the treatise asking whether heretics are to be persecuted, and answered that they are not; the dictionary holds Servetus's denial of the Trinity to be a damning error and holds that Geneva was wrong to burn him, and records that Castellio, whose own views of Scripture and of free will the dictionary does not share, was right on this point. The parable of the tares is to the purpose, where the householder forbids the uprooting, “lest while ye gather up the tares, ye root up also the wheat with them” (Mat 13:29).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the instrument given the church against error is the word, which is sharper than any magistrate's sentence: “the word of God is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword” (Heb 4:12). The caution about judging another man's servant stands over the whole quarrel, “Who art thou that judgest another man's servant?” (Rom 14:4). Basel's real weapon was its presses, and the promise over that work is that the word “shall not return unto me void” (Isa 55:11).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek zao rendered quick or living, Greek logos (G3056), a word; Greek zizanion (G2215), tares; Hebrew dabar (H1697), a word.

expand to see more

Greek logos (G3056) — a word, a saying, a discourse; “the word of God is quick, and powerful”, Hebrews 4:12.

Greek tomoteros (G5114) — sharper, more cutting; “sharper than any twoedged sword”, Hebrews 4:12.

Greek zizanion (G2215) — tares, a weed resembling wheat; “lest while ye gather up the tares”, Matthew 13:29.

Greek oiketes (G3610) — a household servant; “Who art thou that judgest another man's servant?”, Romans 14:4.

Hebrew reyqam (H7387) — empty, without effect; “it shall not return unto me void”, Isaiah 55:11.

Usage

"“the word of God is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword” (Heb 4:12) — the Froben Greek New Testament of 1516."

"“lest while ye gather up the tares, ye root up also the wheat with them” (Mat 13:29) — Castellio against the burning of heretics, 1554."

"“it shall not return unto me void” (Isa 55:11) — a city that printed what no other city would."
